title: This Scientist Says He Can Stop Aging in 3 Years!
summary:
Imagine a pill that could make you feel 25 again—forever. That's what one scientist says he's working on. William "Bill" Andrews, a 74-year-old molecular biologist, claims he's close to creating an anti-aging pill. He says he just needs funding to make it happen.

Andrews's mission started when he was 10. His father told him, "Living is the greatest thing that ever happened to us. When you grow up, you should become a doctor and find a cure for aging." From then on, Andrews had one goal.

His idea focuses on telomeres—tiny protectors at the ends of chromosomes, our DNA packages. Think of them like the plastic tips on shoelaces. Over time, they wear down, and cells stop dividing. That's aging. But an enzyme called telomerase can rebuild telomeres, like hitting a reset button.

The catch? Telomerase is only active in certain cells, like reproductive cells, stem cells, and cancer cells. Andrews wants to find a way to switch it on in all cells. He believes that could stop diseases like cancer, heart disease, and dementia.

Some scientists might disagree, but Andrews is determined. He says aging isn't necessary for humans anymore because we have houses, medicine, and desk jobs. "It will make us younger in every way imaginable—make us look, feel, and behave like we're 25 again," he claims.

Will he succeed? Only time will tell. But it's a fascinating idea!
why_it_matters: Big claims about living forever are exciting, but scientists need evidence before we believe them — asking 'how do they know that?' is a skill you can use at school and in everyday life.

background_read: Telomeres and telomerase were discovered by scientists Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider, who won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for that work.
Many scientists warn that switching on telomerase in every cell could be risky, because cancer cells already use telomerase to keep growing and spreading.

Lots of researchers study aging — some look at diet, exercise and medicines that help people stay healthy for longer — but no pill has been proven to stop aging, and Andrews says he still needs funding (money from supporters) before he can test his idea.
Article_Structure: WHO: William 'Bill' Andrews, a 74-year-old molecular biologist who says he is close to an anti-aging pill
WHAT: He wants to switch on the enzyme telomerase in all cells so telomeres are rebuilt instead of wearing down
WHERE: His idea grew out of a promise he made to his father when he was 10, and he now needs funding to make it happen
WHY: He believes stopping aging could also stop diseases like cancer, heart disease and dementia — though some scientists may disagree

perspectives.description: They think Andrews's idea is inspiring: if aging could be slowed, people might live longer, healthier lives with fewer diseases.
They say no one has shown this works, and aging is caused by many things in the body, not just telomeres wearing down.
They point out that cancer cells use telomerase to grow, so switching it on everywhere could be dangerous rather than helpful.
